---
title: "Week 11 Tutorial: Logistic Regression and GLMs"
subtitle: "Wednesday tutorial · reinforces Monday's lecture on generalized linear models"
toc: true
---



## Goals

-   Recognize when a binary or count outcome needs something other than `lm()`
-   Fit and interpret a logistic regression (`glm` with a binomial family)
-   Get a first look at Poisson regression for count data

## Setup



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
```
:::



## Why not just use `lm()`?

A linear model fit to a 0/1 outcome can predict probabilities below 0 or above 1, and violates the constant-variance assumption near the extremes. **Logistic regression** models the log-odds of the outcome instead.

## Logistic regression: survival example



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(11)
n <- 100
seedlings <- tibble(
  light = runif(n, 0, 100),  # % canopy light
  survived = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-3 + 0.06 * light))
)
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(seedlings, aes(light, survived)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.05, alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Raw survival outcomes vs. light availability](week11-tutorial_files/figure-html/fig-raw-1.png){#fig-raw width=672}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m1 <- glm(survived ~ light, data = seedlings, family = binomial)
summary(m1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Call:
glm(formula = survived ~ light, family = binomial, data = seedlings)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept) -4.17017    0.79104  -5.272 1.35e-07 ***
light        0.08332    0.01608   5.181 2.21e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 133.750  on 99  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance:  79.882  on 98  degrees of freedom
AIC: 83.882

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5
```


:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tidy(m1, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE)  # odds ratios
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 x 7
  term        estimate std.error statistic     p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>       <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)   0.0154    0.791      -5.27 0.000000135  0.00266    0.0616
2 light         1.09      0.0161      5.18 0.000000221  1.06       1.13  
```


:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(seedlings, aes(light, survived)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.05, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "binomial"), se = TRUE) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Fitted probability of survival by light level](week11-tutorial_files/figure-html/fig-fit-1.png){#fig-fit width=672}
:::
:::



::: callout-note
## Exercise 1

Interpret the exponentiated `light` coefficient (the odds ratio) in one sentence a non-statistician biologist would understand.
:::

## Poisson regression: a first look at count data



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(12)
counts <- tibble(
  density = runif(60, 1, 10),   # plants per m^2
  seed_count = rpois(60, lambda = exp(0.5 + 0.15 * density))
)

m2 <- glm(seed_count ~ density, data = counts, family = poisson)
summary(m2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Call:
glm(formula = seed_count ~ density, family = poisson, data = counts)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)  0.43512    0.17806   2.444   0.0145 *  
density      0.16351    0.02621   6.238 4.44e-10 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for poisson family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 81.263  on 59  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 40.970  on 58  degrees of freedom
AIC: 230.66

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4
```


:::
:::



::: callout-note
## Exercise 2

Fit `m2` and report whether `density` significantly predicts `seed_count`. Then check for overdispersion by comparing the residual deviance to the residual degrees of freedom (`summary(m2)` prints both) — a ratio well above 1 suggests you'd want a quasi-Poisson or negative binomial model instead. Is that the case here?
:::

## Choosing a model by outcome type

::: callout-note
## Exercise 3

For each scenario below, name the outcome type and the model you'd reach for (`lm`, logistic `glm`, or Poisson/negative-binomial `glm`):

a.  Number of eggs laid per clutch
b.  Whether a seed germinates (yes/no)
c.  Body mass in grams
d.  Number of parasites found on an individual host
:::
